source.title: Sparser, Better, Deeper, Stronger: Improving Sparse Training with Exact Orthogonal Initialization
source.authors: A. Nowak; Lukasz Gniecki; Filip Szatkowski; Jacek Tabor

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; some figure values are not numerically recoverable from the text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper trains sparse networks from random orthogonal initialization and reports loss curves and accuracy, bearing on initialization and trainability, but it studies static sparse training rather than the claim versions’ full recipes.
record.gate_note: Rows below record the paper’s own training-loss or training-accuracy results. Test-accuracy tables do not measure training classification error and are omitted. Jacobian singular values, runtime comparisons, and cited prior-work results are not outcomes for the versions’ training-error measure. Several training-loss comparisons are figure-only.
record.test_reason: The study extends initialization-dependent learning speed and very-deep plain-network trainability to static sparse networks. Its training-loss comparisons test V4, and its successful 1000-layer tanh experiments bear on the special-initialization clause of V3. Neither claim requires near-zero training classification error for these parts.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that EOI improves static sparse training and enables highly sparse 1000-layer plain MLPs and CNNs without shortcuts or normalization. Their broader language about consistent improvement should be read alongside the reported exceptions.
record.recipe_differences: Uses static sparse training with exact orthogonal initialization (EOI), comparing it with baseline sparse masks and approximate isometry; it does not test the original versions’ specified training-error recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization scheme, activation function, sparsity, density-distribution method, and Givens rotation angle affect reported training dynamics or performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Small-angle Givens initialization gives worse early training loss than random-angle or large-angle initialization in sparse ResNet32, despite competitive final test accuracies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The rotation-angle distribution affects early optimization in sparse residual networks even when initialization remains orthogonal.

fits_no_version.finding: Test-accuracy comparisons on contemporary residual and normalized architectures show architecture-, activation-, density- and mask-dependent benefits from EOI.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse orthogonal initialization can improve generalization performance, with exceptions depending on the architecture and sparse initialization recipe.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235, 2024
record.problems: Training-loss curves are shown in figures without numeric values; the text gives only qualitative descriptions for most of these comparisons. The paper reports test accuracy for its main network experiments rather than training classification error. Each experiment was conducted five times; accuracy tables include standard deviations.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible rows retained. Training-loss curves in Figure 2 and Figure 6 are figure-only; the text describes some aggregate trends but does not give condition-specific values for individual subjects and conditions. Figure 9 describes initial training-loss differences by angle but provides final test accuracy only. Tables 1, 2, 4, and 5 report test accuracy, which does not directly measure the claim’s training-error outcome.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including random or corrupted labels.
Teacher-student ReLU local minima and the effect of adding student neurons.
Depth-induced training-error degradation in plain batch-normalized CNNs, its prevention by identity shortcuts, and Fixup.
Orthogonal versus Gaussian weights at matched variance in very deep tanh networks, a trainable-depth sweep, and 10,000-layer CNNs.
Learning rates relative to the stability threshold, curvature evolution, recovery and divergence.
Controlled batch-normalization comparisons of training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: There are no extracted rows to fix. The record incorrectly treats V4's training-speed and trainability evidence as requiring training classification error. Qualitative training-loss findings are eligible evidence even without recoverable numerical curve values. Successful deep-network learning also bears on trainability, although test accuracy cannot establish zero training error. The relevant omitted experiments are already declared in rows_left_out, so missing is empty. Verdicts explicitly identify their textual basis.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report training classification error, CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training error, or random/corrupted-label memorization.
No two-layer teacher-student local-minimum experiment or width sweep.
Does not compare plain and residual networks for training error; its very deep networks are sparse and tanh, and results are not stated as training classification error.

Tests initialization effects on training dynamics and deep-network trainability, but the training-loss outcomes are figure-only, without a textual description identifying the individual measured conditions and values.
No above-stability-limit learning-rate experiment or sharpness measurement.
No batch-normalization comparison measuring training speed or learning-rate tolerance.
